questions.q: How does this lesson reframe the scalability ceiling that was introduced back in Chapter 2?
options: As a problem that has already been fully solved by RLHF
As an active design problem to be worked on, rather than just an honest limitation to acknowledge
As a concern that only applies to models trained before 2020
As something unrelated to oversight or evaluation
questions.explain: Chapter 2 named the ceiling as a limit on existing methods; this chapter treats the same fact as something scalable oversight techniques actively try to address.

questions.q: What is the general abstract structure of the scalable oversight problem?
options: A strong supervisor training an even stronger system with no verification needed
A weak supervisor — human or a weaker AI standing in for one — needing to provide a reliable training or evaluation signal for a more capable system
Two identical models trained on exactly the same data
A human supervisor who is always more capable than the system being trained
questions.explain: This is the generalized weak-to-strong setup that debate, recursive reward modeling, weak-to-strong generalization, and AI-assisted oversight are all proposed answers to.

questions.q: Why does ordinary RLHF-style direct judgment break down once a task exceeds the judge's verification ability?
options: Because RLHF requires more compute than any other training method
Because the judge can no longer reliably tell which output is actually better, so the judgment signal becomes unreliable in ways that are hard to detect from outside
Because RLHF only works on tasks with no correct answer at all
Because direct judgment always rewards the worst possible output
questions.explain: Direct judgment depends on the judge's ability to verify quality; once that ability is exceeded, the signal can degrade without an obvious external sign.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by the "verification-generation gap"?
options: The idea that generating an answer and checking it require the same amount of effort in every case
The difference in effort or difficulty between checking whether an answer is correct and producing that answer in the first place
A gap in training data between generation tasks and verification tasks
The time delay between a model generating an output and a human reading it
questions.explain: Scalable oversight techniques try to exploit the fact that verifying correctness can sometimes be easier than generating the correct answer from scratch.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what do debate, recursive reward modeling, weak-to-strong generalization, and AI-assisted human oversight have in common?
options: They are all different proposed answers to the same weak-supervisor, strong-system oversight problem
They are all mutually exclusive techniques that cannot be studied in the same course
They all require discarding RLHF entirely before they can be used
They were all developed by the exact same research team at the same lab
questions.explain: Each technique approaches the same abstract problem from a different leverage point, as this chapter's remaining lessons cover in turn.
